definition.text: A natural resource, also called a finite resource, that nature cannot replace quickly enough to keep up with how fast people use it.

facts.text: Minerals and metal ores, fossil fuels (coal, petroleum, natural gas) and groundwater in some aquifers are all non-renewable.
Ore deposits form only where geological processes concentrate metals, which takes tens of thousands to millions of years, so near-surface deposits are non-renewable on human time-frames.
Coal, oil and gas take thousands of years to form and cannot be replaced as fast as they are used; fossil fuels are the main energy source humans use today.
Some argue carbon fuel is practically inexhaustible if methane hydrates on the sea floor are counted, though whether they can be extracted at viable cost is unknown.
In economics, a non-renewable resource is a good where using more today means less is available tomorrow.
David Ricardo argued that a mineral's price should rise over time, with the costliest mine setting the price and cheaper mines earning a differential rent.
Without regulation, people and firms tend to keep using non-renewable resources because the easier, cheaper option often differs from the environmentally friendly one.

definition.text: The idea that land can be reused but not created on demand, so economists treat it as a fixed resource whose supply cannot respond to price.

facts.text: Land surface can count as either renewable or non-renewable depending on what it is compared with.
In economic terms land has perfectly inelastic supply.
Unlike capital goods, land and non-renewable resources cannot be produced or increased.

definition.text: The question of whether nuclear fuels should count as renewable, since mined uranium is finite but breeder reactors make more fuel than they use.

facts.text: In 1987 the World Commission on Environment and Development classed breeder reactors, which produce more fissile fuel than they consume, as renewable energy sources.
Uranium, the most common fission fuel, occurs at low concentrations and is mined in 19 countries.
Nuclear power provides about 6% of the world's energy and 13–14% of its electricity.
Nuclear plants produce about 10,000 metric tons of high level waste each year worldwide, which is hazardous if not properly contained.

definition.text: A natural resource, also called a flow resource, that replaces what is used up through natural reproduction or other recurring processes within a human time scale.

facts.text: Resources whose recovery is unlikely ever to exceed a human time scale are called perpetual resources.
Water, forests, plants and animals are renewable only as long as they are adequately monitored, protected and conserved.
Water stays renewable only when its use is carefully controlled; groundwater pumped far faster than it recharges counts as non-renewable.
Sun, wind, water movement and geothermal heat are practically infinite and cannot be depleted.
Unregulated industrial growth endangers renewable resources, which must be managed so use does not exceed nature's capacity to replenish them.
Overuse of renewables such as deforestation, overgrazing and overfishing was already a large problem in early modern times.
An unregulated industry practice can lead to complete depletion of a renewable resource, as overfishing shows.
Building renewable energy devices still uses non-renewable resources such as mined metals and land.
